title: Glucose, ketones and lactate
subtitle: Hypoglycaemia, DKA/euglycaemic DKA, HHS and lactate patterns
summary: Hypoglycaemia, DKA/euglycaemic DKA, HHS and lactate patterns
introduction: Interpret glucose with symptoms, diabetes type, medication, food intake, illness and ketones. SGLT2 inhibitors can produce euglycaemic DKA: ketoacidosis with glucose that is normal or only mildly raised.

rows.name: Hypoglycaemia
rows.referenceRange: RVH fasting glucose reference: 4.1–6.1 mmol/L; the clinical hypoglycaemia threshold remains <4.0 mmol/L
notes: Treat promptly when symptomatic or below 4.0 mmol/L. Examples include sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, behavioural change, confusion, seizure or reduced consciousness. Recheck after treatment and identify the cause.

rows.name: Marked hyperglycaemia
rows.referenceRange: No single value diagnoses DKA or HHS
notes: Assess ketones, pH/bicarbonate, osmolality, hydration, cognition and precipitating illness. Polyuria, polydipsia, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or shock require urgent assessment.

rows.name: Blood ketones
rows.referenceRange: RVH fasting 3-hydroxybutyrate reference: 0.03–0.3 mmol/L; retain DKA decision thresholds separately
notes: DKA is supported by ketonaemia ≥3.0 mmol/L with acidosis (venous pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <15 mmol/L) and diabetes/hyperglycaemia. Do not dismiss DKA because glucose is below 11 mmol/L, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy or reduced food intake.

rows.name: Possible HHS
rows.referenceRange: Often glucose ≥30 mmol/L and calculated osmolality ≥320 mOsm/kg
notes: Look for profound dehydration, reduced cognition, focal neurology, seizures, hypotension and minimal ketonaemia. Mixed DKA/HHS can occur.

rows.name: Raised lactate
rows.referenceRange: RVH lactate reference: 0.5–2.2 mmol/L; >4.0 mmol/L is a critical-result alert threshold
notes: Consider hypoperfusion, sepsis, seizure, severe work of breathing, beta-agonists, liver dysfunction, metformin accumulation, toxins or sampling delay. A normal lactate does not exclude sepsis or shock.

urgentFindings: Glucose below 4.0 mmol/L with confusion, seizure, reduced consciousness or failure to respond to treatment.
Ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L, or ketones ≥1.5 mmol/L with vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, drowsiness or clinical dehydration.
Suspected euglycaemic DKA in an unwell patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor, even when glucose is not markedly raised.
Lactate ≥4.0 mmol/L, a rising lactate, hypotension, mottled skin, reduced urine output or new confusion.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Classic DKA picture
interpretation: Meets the classic biochemical picture of DKA; severity and disposition depend on the degree of acidosis, conscious level, potassium and precipitating illness, not glucose alone
actions: Treat as time-critical per local DKA pathway (see urgent findings)
Request U&E urgently — potassium management is central to safe DKA treatment and can change rapidly with treatment
Identify and treat the precipitant (infection, missed insulin, new diagnosis, illness) alongside DKA management

commonPatterns.title: Euglycaemic DKA picture
findings: Glucose normal or only mildly raised (below the level usually expected for DKA)
SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy, reduced food intake, or prolonged fasting/vomiting
interpretation: Euglycaemic DKA can be missed if glucose alone is used to screen for DKA — SGLT2 inhibitors in particular can produce significant ketoacidosis with a near-normal glucose
The ketone and acid-base picture, not the glucose, defines this presentation
actions: Do not dismiss DKA because glucose is below 11 mmol/L, particularly with SGLT2 inhibitor use, pregnancy or reduced food intake (see urgent findings)
Ask specifically about SGLT2 inhibitor use, recent reduced intake, vomiting or intercurrent illness
Treat as time-critical per local DKA pathway once identified, adjusting fluid/insulin approach for the near-normal glucose as per local protocol

commonPatterns.title: Possible HHS picture
findings: Profound dehydration, reduced cognition or focal neurology
interpretation: Suggests hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state rather than DKA; HHS carries a high mortality and needs a different fluid/insulin approach to DKA, with much greater caution around the rate of osmolality correction
Mixed DKA/HHS can occur, so ketones and acid-base status should still be checked even when the picture looks like HHS
actions: Treat as time-critical and arrange urgent hospital assessment (see urgent findings)
Request U&E and osmolality (measured or calculated) to confirm the degree of hyperosmolarity and guide fluid management (see further testing)
Assess for seizures, focal neurology and hypotension, and monitor closely as osmolality corrects

commonPatterns.title: Hypoglycaemia with an identifiable cause
findings: Known insulin or sulfonylurea use, missed meal, alcohol, exercise or intercurrent illness
interpretation: Most hypoglycaemia in known diabetics has an identifiable precipitant (medication timing/dose, missed food, exercise, alcohol, renal impairment affecting drug clearance)
Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia can be prolonged and recurrent, unlike a single insulin-related episode, and needs longer observation
actions: Treat promptly per local hypoglycaemia protocol and recheck glucose after treatment (see urgent findings)
Identify the precipitant and address it (dose/timing review, food intake, alcohol) before discharge/handover
Extend observation or arrange medical review if a sulfonylurea or long-acting insulin is involved, given the risk of recurrence

commonPatterns.title: Raised lactate — hypoperfusion or sepsis
findings: Hypotension, tachycardia, mottled skin, reduced urine output or signs of infection
interpretation: Supports significant hypoperfusion or sepsis and is an important marker of illness severity, but a normal lactate does not exclude sepsis or shock, and a raised lactate can also occur with seizure, severe work of breathing, beta-agonist use, liver dysfunction, metformin accumulation or toxins
actions: Treat as time-critical if lactate is ≥4.0 mmol/L, rising, or accompanied by hypotension, mottled skin, reduced urine output or new confusion (see urgent findings)
Consider non-hypoperfusion causes (seizure, salbutamol, metformin, liver disease) if the clinical picture does not fit sepsis/shock
Repeat lactate to assess trend and response to treatment (see further testing)

rationale: Confirms and quantifies acidosis, which is central to diagnosing and grading the severity of DKA alongside ketones
Potassium management is a core part of safe DKA/HHS treatment, and renal function informs fluid resuscitation and drug clearance (e.g. metformin accumulation causing lactic acidosis)
Confirms and quantifies hyperosmolarity in suspected HHS, guiding the safe rate of correction
Helps identify infection as a precipitant of DKA, HHS or a raised lactate
Trend over serial results helps distinguish a transient or artefactual rise from ongoing hypoperfusion, and shows response to treatment
Identifies ECG changes of hyperkalaemia or hypokalaemia, which are relevant both at presentation and during DKA/HHS treatment as potassium shifts

specimens.notes: Plasma — grey-top sodium-fluoride EDTA tube. RVH specifies 4 mL for glucose; lactate should reach the laboratory within 30 minutes.
